set1.q: A 64-year-old man is admitted with an inferior myocardial infarction. His heart rate falls to 46 with narrow QRS complexes and P waves that are either inverted (retrograde P waves) or buried in the QRS. Which rhythm is most likely?
opts: Atrial flutter
Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, not inverted P waves at 46.
Focal atrial tachycardia
Focal atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm above 100 from one atrial focus; his rhythm is slow at 46.
Junctional rhythm
Correct. A regular narrow rhythm at 40 to 60 with inverted or buried P waves is a junctional rhythm, and inferior myocardial infarction is a listed cause.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia keeps an upright, normal P wave before each QRS; his are inverted or buried.

set1.q: A 74-year-old woman with decompensated heart failure and chronic lung disease develops an irregular tachycardia with three different P-wave shapes in one lead. What does this rhythm signal about her course?
opts: A pacemaker is needed
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; multifocal atrial tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying illness and signals a poor prognosis.
A poor prognosis
Correct. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a poor prognostic sign, occurring in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure and right heart stress.
A benign finding
Benign describes focal atrial tachycardia; multifocal atrial tachycardia signals serious underlying illness.
Imminent recovery
Multifocal atrial tachycardia marks acute illness with right heart stress, not recovery, and carries a poor prognosis.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man with a slow sinus rhythm at 34 is hypotensive and drowsy. Two doses of atropine have not changed his rate or blood pressure. Which is the next step?
opts: Oral metoprolol
A beta blocker is a cause of bradycardia, not a rescue for it; the next step after atropine is a temporary pacemaker.
Temporary pacemaker
Correct. When atropine fails in acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia, the next step is a temporary pacemaker; a permanent pacemaker follows if the cause will not resolve.
Adenosine
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node and would slow him further; after failed atropine, a temporary pacemaker is used.
Synchronized cardioversion
A synchronized shock is for unstable fast rhythms; a slow rhythm unresponsive to atropine needs temporary pacing.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man has a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 210. His blood pressure is 72/40, and he is confused and sweating. Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
opts: Vagal maneuver
A vagal maneuver is first line only for the stable patient; hypotension with confusion calls for immediate synchronized cardioversion.
Adenosine
Adenosine is for the stable patient after a vagal maneuver; this patient is unstable and needs synchronized cardioversion.
Unsynchronized defibrillation
Defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms; he has a pulse, so the shock must be synchronized.
Synchronized cardioversion
Correct. Hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia (hypotension and confusion) gets immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage.

set1.q: A 47-year-old woman has persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions despite cutting out caffeine and alcohol. She has no contraindications to beta blockade. Which treatment is first?
opts: Warfarin
Warfarin is an anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation; it does nothing for premature atrial beats.
Metoprolol
Correct. Persistent, symptomatic premature atrial contractions are treated with a beta blocker such as metoprolol if not contraindicated.
Procainamide
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White; symptomatic premature atrial beats get a beta blocker.
Adenosine
Adenosine acts for seconds to stop reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; it cannot suppress premature beats.

set1.q: A 73-year-old man has new pauses and slow rates on an ambulatory monitor. He started verapamil and digoxin last month for palpitations. He feels mildly lightheaded but is otherwise well. Which is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Catheter ablation
Ablation targets a tachycardia focus or pathway; his slow rates and pauses come from rate-slowing drugs.
Atropine tablets
Atropine is an acute intravenous rescue for unstable bradycardia, not a long-term oral therapy; stopping the culprit drugs comes first.
Stop the rate-slowing drugs
Correct. Medications (beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin) are listed causes of sick sinus syndrome, and management starts by treating the underlying cause.
Permanent pacemaker now
A pacemaker may be needed if symptomatic bradycardia persists, but a reversible drug cause is addressed first.

set1.q: A 16-year-old boy has a delta wave (a slurred upstroke of the QRS) with a short PR interval on a screening electrocardiogram but no symptoms. His parents ask what the finding means. Which explanation is most accurate?
opts: A slow node needing a pacemaker
Pre-excitation speeds conduction to the ventricles through an extra pathway; it is not a slow node that needs pacing.
An extra pathway causing fast rhythms
Correct. Pre-excitation with a delta wave means an accessory pathway (the bundle of Kent), which carries the potential for reentrant tachycardia, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White.
A sign of a prior heart attack
Infarction changes the ST segment and Q waves; a short PR with a delta wave reflects an accessory pathway.
A normal athletic heart
Athletic hearts show sinus bradycardia or junctional rhythm; a delta wave is an accessory pathway, not training.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man with stable atrial fibrillation at 92 asks why the plan is to control his heart rate rather than shock him back into normal rhythm today. Which explanation is most accurate?
opts: His rhythm can never be restored
Rhythm can be restored by cardioversion or ablation later; today the first goal is rate control.
Slowing the rate dissolves clots
Rate control does not dissolve clots; anticoagulation, guided by stroke risk, is what addresses clots.
Rate control is the first goal
Correct. In hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation the first goal is rate control, with anticoagulation; elective cardioversion can follow after 21 days of anticoagulation.
Shocks are never used for it
Synchronized cardioversion is used, both for instability and electively after 21 days of anticoagulation.

set1.q: A 34-year-old woman is brought in after a car crash with a heart rate of 128 and a blood pressure of 88/56. The rhythm is regular with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Bedside ultrasound shows free fluid in the abdomen. Which is the most appropriate approach to her heart rate?
opts: Intravenous metoprolol
Slowing a compensatory tachycardia in a hypovolemic patient would remove her compensation; the bleeding is what needs treatment.
Treat the blood loss
Correct. This is appropriate sinus tachycardia from hypovolemia, a pathologic cause; management of appropriate sinus tachycardia is treating the underlying cause.
Adenosine
Adenosine is for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; a sinus tachycardia compensating for blood loss settles when the cause is treated.
Synchronized cardioversion
Cardioversion cannot fix a compensatory sinus rhythm and would not restore her volume; the cause must be treated.

set1.q: A 30-year-old woman with a stable, regular narrow complex tachycardia at 180 is being treated in the emergency department. She is alert with a normal blood pressure. Which treatment should be avoided at this stage?
opts: Unsynchronized defibrillation

Correct. Unsynchronized defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms; a stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine, and only an unstable one with synchronized cardioversion.
Vagal maneuver
A vagal maneuver is the first-line step for stable supraventricular tachycardia, not something to avoid.
Adenosine
Adenosine is the second step after a failed vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia.
A second adenosine dose
Adenosine may be given twice as needed in stable supraventricular tachycardia, so a second dose is appropriate.

set1.q: A 34-year-old woman has frequent, disruptive episodes of atrioventricular nodal reentry and wants a definitive cure. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Catheter ablation
Correct. Catheter ablation offers a select subset of patients with nodal reentry the opportunity for a definitive cure, in over 95%.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms such as sick sinus syndrome; nodal reentry is cured by catheter ablation.
Valve replacement
Nodal reentry usually occurs without heart disease, in structurally normal hearts; valve surgery has no role.
Septal myectomy
Myectomy relieves outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it does not treat nodal reentry.

set1.q: A 24-year-old man is told his electrocardiogram shows a normal P wave before each narrow QRS at 68 beats per minute, with the rate rising as he breathes in and falling as he breathes out. He worries that he has heart disease. Which counseling is most accurate?
opts: A normal variant; no treatment
Correct. A sinus rate that speeds with inspiration and slows with expiration, with normal P waves and a narrow QRS, is sinus arrhythmia, a normal physiologic variant that needs no treatment.
He needs a pacemaker workup
Pacemakers are for symptomatic bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome or high-grade block; a breathing-linked sinus variation is normal and needs nothing.
He should stop exercising
Exercise restriction has no place here; sinus arrhythmia is a normal physiologic response to breathing.
He needs an anticoagulant
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; sinus arrhythmia carries no clot risk and needs no treatment.

set1.q: A 75-year-old man has a junctional rhythm at 42 with dizziness. Monitoring shows that the cause is high-grade atrioventricular block. Which treatment is indicated?
opts: Observation
Observation suits an asymptomatic healthy person; a symptomatic junctional rhythm from high-grade block needs a pacemaker.
Adenosine
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node further and would worsen the high-grade block causing his rhythm.
Catheter ablation
Ablation treats tachycardias; a junctional escape from high-grade block needs pacing.
Permanent pacemaker
Correct. A junctional rhythm due to complete or high-grade atrioventricular block or sick sinus syndrome is treated with a permanent pacemaker.

set1.q: A 33-year-old woman has abrupt-onset palpitations during a week of little sleep and heavy coffee. Her heart rate is 160 and regular, and every QRS is preceded by an identical P wave whose shape differs from her baseline P wave. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with at least three P-wave shapes, usually in severe lung disease or heart failure.
Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia keeps the patient's normal P-wave shape; a consistent abnormal P wave means an ectopic atrial focus.
Atrial flutter
Flutter shows sawtooth waves at 250 or more per minute, not a single abnormal P wave before each QRS at 160.
Focal atrial tachycardia

Correct. A regular tachycardia with one consistent, abnormally shaped P wave before each QRS, starting abruptly in someone without heart disease under increased metabolic demand, is focal atrial tachycardia.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man has frequent premature atrial contractions on a monitor (early beats with abnormal P waves), many per minute. He has no known heart disease. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
opts: Test for an accessory pathway
An accessory pathway is suspected with a short PR and delta wave; frequent premature atrial beats prompt a structural workup.
Serum digoxin level
Digoxin toxicity is a cause of junctional rhythm; he takes no digoxin, and frequent premature atrial beats call for a structural workup.
No evaluation is needed
Infrequent, asymptomatic beats need nothing, but frequent ones prompt a search for structural heart disease.
Look for structural heart disease
Correct. If premature atrial contractions are frequent, look for underlying structural heart disease; in a diseased heart they may precede supraventricular tachycardia, fibrillation or flutter.

set1.q: A 72-year-old woman with symptomatic sinus bradycardia at 45 also has hypertension that needs a new medication. Which antihypertensive should be avoided?
opts: Losartan
Losartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker, does not slow the heart; verapamil does and should be avoided.
Verapamil
Correct. Verapamil is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, and these drugs, like beta blockers and digoxin, cause sinus bradycardia; it would slow her further.
Lisinopril
Lisinopril does not slow the sinus node and is not among the listed causes of bradycardia, so it is not the drug to avoid.
Chlorthalidone
A thiazide-type diuretic does not cause sinus bradycardia; the drugs to avoid are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation at 150 has crackles throughout both lungs from pulmonary edema and a blood pressure of 82/50. Which feature makes this presentation a medical emergency?
opts: Her age over 65
Older age raises atrial fibrillation risk but does not make a presentation an emergency; severe heart failure does.
Pulmonary edema with hypotension
Correct. Medical emergencies from atrial fibrillation include severe heart failure (pulmonary edema, hypotension) and atrial fibrillation with an acute myocardial infarction.
A heart rate above 100
A rate above 100 is rapid ventricular response, which needs rate control but is not by itself the listed emergency.
An irregularly irregular pulse
An irregularly irregular pulse defines atrial fibrillation and is not itself the emergency.

set1.q: A 72-year-old woman has sinus pauses of up to 2 seconds at night on an ambulatory monitor. Her occasional dizziness happens only when she stands up quickly and never during the pauses. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Permanent pacemaker
A permanent pacemaker is for symptomatic bradycardia; her dizziness does not match her pauses, so observation is appropriate.
Atropine
Atropine is for acute, symptomatic, unstable bradycardia; she is neither unstable nor symptomatic during the pauses.
Catheter ablation
Ablation treats tachycardias from a focus or pathway; it has no role in brief, asymptomatic sinus pauses.
Observation
Correct. In sick sinus syndrome, management confirms whether symptoms correlate with the bradycardia; when they do not, observation is appropriate.

set1.q: An 81-year-old man has known tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) and asks which fast rhythm is behind his palpitations. An ambulatory monitor is arranged. Which rhythm is it most likely to record during the fast episodes?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia can occur in some patients, who then need a defibrillator with the pacemaker, but atrial fibrillation is the most common.
Junctional rhythm
A junctional rhythm is a slow escape rhythm (usually 40 to 60), not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. In tachy-brady syndrome the tachyarrhythmia that alternates with bradycardia or pauses is most commonly atrial fibrillation.
Atrial flutter
Flutter is an organized atrial circuit with sawtooth waves; it is not the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.

set1.q: A 79-year-old man has tachy-brady syndrome (a fast rhythm alternating with slow rates and pauses) on monitoring, and he faints during the pauses. Thyroid tests and electrolytes are normal and he takes no rate-slowing drugs. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Atropine as needed
Atropine is a short-acting rescue for acute unstable bradycardia, not long-term protection against pauses.
Catheter ablation alone
Ablation does nothing for the failing sinus node that causes his pauses; he needs a permanent pacemaker.
Observation alone
Observation is appropriate only when symptoms do not correlate with the bradycardia; his fainting during pauses needs a pacemaker.
Permanent pacemaker
Correct. When symptoms correlate with bradycardia in sick sinus syndrome a permanent pacemaker is placed, and tachy-brady syndrome often needs one.

set1.q: A 62-year-old man started a new blood pressure medication two weeks ago. He now feels tired, and his pulse is 46 and regular, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Thyroid tests are normal. Which medication is the most likely cause?
opts: Metoprolol
Correct. Beta blockers such as metoprolol, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin are the drug causes of sinus bradycardia; a new one two weeks ago is the likely culprit.
Amlodipine
Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker; the calcium channel blockers that cause bradycardia are the nondihydropyridines, verapamil and diltiazem.
Lisinopril
Lisinopril, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, is not among the drug causes of sinus bradycardia; beta blockers are.
Hydrochlorothiazide
A thiazide diuretic does not slow the sinus node; the listed bradycardic drugs are beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman has a slow sinus rhythm at 38 six hours after an inferior myocardial infarction. She feels faint and her blood pressure is 80/50. Each narrow QRS has a normal P wave before it. Which drug should be given first?
opts: Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, another drug cause of bradycardia; it would worsen her hypotension and slow rate.
Adenosine
Adenosine stops supraventricular tachycardia by blocking the atrioventricular node; it has no place in an unstable bradycardia.
Atropine
Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia, here from an infarction affecting the conduction tissue, is treated first with atropine, then a temporary pacemaker.
Metoprolol
Metoprolol is a beta blocker, a listed cause of sinus bradycardia; it would slow her further.

set1.q: A 57-year-old woman has frequent premature junctional contractions, more than 10 per minute, on a monitor. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Check for heart disease
Correct. Frequent premature junctional contractions (more than 10 per minute, or multifocal) prompt a search for structural heart disease, with a beta blocker to treat them.
Reassurance only
Reassurance alone suits infrequent, asymptomatic junctional beats; frequent ones need a structural workup.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; frequent premature beats prompt a structural workup.
Anticoagulation
Anticoagulation is for atrial fibrillation and flutter, not premature junctional beats.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation started an antiarrhythmic and then develops atrial flutter. Suddenly her ventricular rate matches her atrial rate at 280, with hypotension. Which complication is she now at high risk of?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is an irregular atrial rhythm of lung disease; the danger of 1:1 flutter is ventricular fibrillation.
Ventricular fibrillation
Correct. 1:1 atrial flutter, where every flutter wave conducts, causes extreme hemodynamic instability and carries a big risk of progression to ventricular fibrillation.
Complete heart block
Complete heart block stops conduction to the ventricles; 1:1 flutter is the opposite, conducting every flutter wave.
Sinus arrest
Sinus arrest is a failure of the sinus node to fire, part of sick sinus syndrome, not the danger of 1:1 flutter.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man had coronary bypass surgery two months ago. He now has palpitations and fatigue. His heart rate is 150 and regular, and the electrocardiogram shows sawtooth flutter waves, two for every narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block
Correct. Sawtooth flutter waves with two for every narrow QRS are atrial flutter with 2:1 block, the most common ratio, and atrial scarring after surgery is a classic setting.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no organized atrial waves; his rhythm is regular with sawtooth waves.
Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia has a normal P wave before each QRS, not two sawtooth waves per QRS.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three or more distinct P-wave shapes, not uniform sawtooth waves.

Correct. Atrioventricular nodal reentry almost always terminates with vagal maneuvers or adenosine; synchronized cardioversion is rarely required.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is rarely required in nodal reentry and is kept for the unstable patient.
Intravenous procainamide
Procainamide is for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, not nodal reentry.
Catheter ablation
Ablation offers a definitive cure for selected patients but is not how an acute episode is stopped.

The rhythm is irregular and wide-complex, at rates up to 260, with varying delta waves (slurred upstrokes). He is alert with a blood pressure of 118/74. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Intravenous magnesium
Magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a long QT, not pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Atropine
Atropine speeds conduction and is for unstable bradycardia; it would accelerate a pre-excited tachycardia.
Intravenous procainamide
Correct. Irregular, wide, very fast complexes in a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White are pre-excited atrial fibrillation, treated with intravenous procainamide; adenosine must never be used.
Adenosine
Adenosine is contraindicated here: it blocks only the normal node and lets the accessory pathway carry the fibrillation.

opts: Intravenous rate control
Correct. A hemodynamically stable patient in atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response gets intravenous rate control; rate control is the first goal.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is for the hemodynamically unstable patient; she is alert with a normal blood pressure.
Immediate ablation
Mapping and ablation is a later, elective rhythm option, not the first treatment of rapid ventricular response.
Intravenous atropine
Atropine speeds the heart and is for unstable bradycardia; it would worsen rapid ventricular response.

opts: Electrical cardioversion
Cardioversion is appropriate if she becomes unstable; the treatment to avoid is adenosine.
Later pathway ablation
Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line chronic treatment for Wolff-Parkinson-White.
Adenosine

Correct. In atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, adenosine must never be used: blocking the normal atrioventricular node leaves the accessory pathway to conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.
Procainamide
Procainamide is the drug of choice for atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, not one to avoid.

4 to 5

set2.q: A 17-year-old basketball player collapses briefly during a game and recovers. In the emergency department he is in sinus rhythm at 78. His electrocardiogram shows a PR interval of 0.10 seconds and a delta wave (a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS) with a widened QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sick sinus syndrome
Sick sinus syndrome causes pauses and tachy-brady swings in older adults; it does not produce a delta wave.
Focal atrial tachycardia
Focal atrial tachycardia gives a fast rhythm with an abnormal P wave; it does not shorten the PR interval or create a delta wave in sinus rhythm.
Wolff-Parkinson-White

Correct. A short PR interval with a delta wave and widened QRS in sinus rhythm is pre-excitation from an accessory pathway (the bundle of Kent): Wolff-Parkinson-White, which classically first shows itself as collapse in a young athlete.
Atrioventricular nodal reentry
Nodal reentry is a circuit inside the atrioventricular node and does not produce a short PR or delta wave in sinus rhythm.

set2.q: A 19-year-old swimmer has an electrocardiogram before a sports physical. She has no symptoms. The rate is 72, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS, but the beats come closer together as she breathes in and spread apart as she breathes out. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus arrhythmia

Correct. A normal P wave before every narrow QRS at 60 to 100, with the rate rising on inspiration and falling on expiration, is sinus arrhythmia: a normal, physiologic rhythm that is irregular with a pattern.
Sick sinus syndrome
Sick sinus syndrome produces pauses, sinus arrest or tachy-brady swings in a diseased node, usually with symptoms; a breathing-linked variation in a healthy swimmer is sinus arrhythmia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast, irregular rhythm with at least three P-wave shapes in acutely ill lung or heart patients; her single P-wave shape at 72 is sinus.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; she has a normal P wave before every beat and a regular pattern tied to breathing.

set2.q: A 45-year-old man has a heart rate of 122 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. His temperature is 39.2°C and he has a productive cough and crackles at the right base. He is alert with a blood pressure of 126/78. Which is the best treatment for his heart rate?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion
Cardioversion is for unstable reentrant or fibrillatory rhythms; this stable sinus tachycardia needs its cause treated.
Treat the infection and fever
Correct. A sinus tachycardia from fever and infection is an appropriate response to a pathologic process, and appropriate sinus tachycardia is managed by treating the underlying cause.
Adenosine
Adenosine stops reentrant supraventricular tachycardia through the atrioventricular node; it has no role in a sinus tachycardia from fever.
Vagal maneuver
Vagal maneuvers are first line for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; a fever-driven sinus tachycardia settles when the infection is treated.

set2.q: A 76-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness and one faint. A 24-hour ambulatory monitor shows runs of a fast, irregular rhythm that alternate with slow rates, and a long pause each time the fast rhythm stops. Which fast rhythm is most likely on her monitor?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation is a pulseless arrest rhythm, not a recurring run she survives; the usual fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome is atrial fibrillation.
Sinus tachycardia
In tachy-brady syndrome the fast rhythm comes from outside the failing sinus node, most commonly atrial fibrillation.
Atrioventricular nodal reentry
Nodal reentry is a regular narrow tachycardia, usually in younger women without heart disease; it is not the fast phase of tachy-brady syndrome.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. Fast rhythms alternating with bradycardia and offset pauses are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome in which the tachyarrhythmia is most commonly atrial fibrillation.

opts: Synchronized cardioversion
Correct. Hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation (hypotension and altered mental status) is treated with synchronized cardioversion.
Intravenous rate control
Intravenous rate control is for the stable patient with rapid ventricular response; this patient is unstable.
Oral rate control
Oral rate control suits a stable patient without rapid ventricular response, not someone hypotensive and confused.
Anticoagulate for 21 days
Three weeks of anticoagulation precedes elective outpatient cardioversion; instability needs cardioversion now.

opts: Intravenous magnesium
Magnesium is the drug for torsades de pointes; stable focal atrial tachycardia gets a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
Intravenous beta blocker
Correct. Stable, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia is treated with an intravenous beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker while the underlying cause is identified and treated.
Intravenous atropine
Atropine speeds the heart and is for unstable bradycardia; it would worsen a fast atrial focus.
Unsynchronized defibrillation
Defibrillation is for pulseless rhythms; a stable patient with focal atrial tachycardia gets intravenous rate control.

opts: Synchronized cardioversion
Cardioversion resets fast rhythms; chronic symptomatic sinus bradycardia needs a permanent pacemaker.
Permanent pacemaker
Correct. Chronic, symptomatic sinus bradycardia with no reversible cause, as here in an older adult, is managed with a permanent pacemaker.
Atropine as needed
Atropine is a short-acting rescue for acute, unstable bradycardia, not long-term therapy for chronic symptomatic disease.
Catheter ablation
Ablation destroys tissue causing a tachycardia; it cannot speed a slow sinus node.

set2.q: A 31-year-old woman has inappropriate sinus tachycardia at about 110 after a full workup excluded other causes. Her only symptom is awareness of her heartbeat, and she asks whether she needs medication. Which response is most accurate?
opts: Usually left untreated; benign

Correct. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is generally left untreated: patients tolerate the symptoms better than the treatment, beta blockers are poorly tolerated, and the prognosis is usually benign.
She needs a lifelong beta blocker
Beta blockers are not well tolerated in inappropriate sinus tachycardia, which is why it is usually left untreated.
Cardioversion will cure it
Cardioversion resets reentrant or fibrillatory rhythms; inappropriate sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm and is usually left untreated.
She needs anticoagulation
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; a sinus tachycardia carries no such need.

opts: HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) score
Correct. The HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) score estimates the risk of major bleeding for patients on anticoagulation, to weigh risk against benefit in atrial fibrillation care.
CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score
The CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation, not the risk of bleeding.
Wells (clot likelihood) score
The Wells score estimates the likelihood of deep vein thrombosis, not bleeding on anticoagulation.
Duke (endocarditis) criteria
The modified Duke criteria classify infective endocarditis; bleeding risk uses the HAS-BLED (bleeding risk) score.

set2.q: A 61-year-old man's frequent premature atrial contractions are shown on monitoring to trigger his episodes of atrial fibrillation. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; premature beats triggering fibrillation are targeted by ablation.
Carotid endarterectomy
Carotid surgery treats carotid artery stenosis; premature atrial beats that trigger fibrillation are ablated.
Septal myectomy
Myectomy treats obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it has no role in premature atrial beats.
Catheter ablation
Correct. Catheter ablation is used if premature atrial contractions are frequent or are triggering atrial fibrillation.

opts: Premature atrial contractions
Isolated premature atrial beats are usually benign; the dangerous rhythm is atrial fibrillation conducting down the pathway.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia is a normal breathing-linked variation in the sinus rate and poses no danger to him.
Atrial fibrillation down the pathway
Correct. Atrial fibrillation conducting down an accessory pathway is the most dangerous combination: it can exceed 200, approaching 300, and cause collapse.
Sinus tachycardia with exercise
Sinus tachycardia is a normal response to exercise and conducts through the normal system at rates up to 160.

opts: ST elevation from infarction
Adenosine is not given to uncover infarction; slowing the ventricular rate shows whether there are hidden P waves.
A prolonged QT interval
QT prolongation is a risk for torsades de pointes; adenosine's diagnostic use in a narrow tachycardia is revealing P waves.
A bundle branch block
A bundle branch block widens the QRS; adenosine slows the ventricular rate to show the hidden atrial activity.
Whether P waves are present
Correct. Adenosine may convert a supraventricular tachycardia to normal sinus rhythm, or at least slow the rate so you can see whether P waves are there.

opts: Stroke from a clot
Correct. Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation prevents stroke; the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke risk) score is used to assess that risk, which rises with age.
Heart block
Anticoagulants do not affect conduction; their purpose in atrial fibrillation is preventing stroke.
Ventricular fibrillation
Anticoagulants do not prevent ventricular arrhythmias; they prevent embolic stroke.
A faster heart rate
Rate control drugs, not anticoagulants, slow the heart; anticoagulants prevent stroke.

Vagal maneuvers are first line for stable supraventricular tachycardia; unstable flutter needs synchronized cardioversion.
Synchronized cardioversion
Correct. Hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter (hypotension with confusion) is treated with synchronized cardioversion.
Oral rate control
Oral rate control is for the stable patient; hypotension and confusion call for synchronized cardioversion.

set2.q: A 20-year-old man is evaluated after a regular tachycardia at 220 that was terminated in the emergency department. An accessory pathway is suspected, but the tachycardia tracing shows no delta wave (slurred upstroke). On which tracing is pre-excitation (a short PR interval with a delta wave) most likely to be seen?
opts: A tracing in sinus rhythm

Correct. Evidence of pre-excitation (short PR interval and delta wave) is found on electrocardiograms taken during normal sinus rhythm; during orthodromic tachycardia the QRS is narrow with no delta wave.
A tracing during tachycardia
During orthodromic reentry the impulse goes down the normal node and back up the pathway, so the QRS is narrow without a delta wave.
A chest radiograph
A chest radiograph does not show electrical pre-excitation; it is seen on an electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm.
An echocardiogram
An echocardiogram shows structure, not the short PR and delta wave of pre-excitation, which appear on a sinus-rhythm electrocardiogram.

set2.q: A 19-year-old woman with Wolff-Parkinson-White has had three emergency visits for reentrant tachycardia this year. Which long-term management is first line?
opts: Lifelong anticoagulation
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation; it does not treat the accessory pathway.
Ablation of the pathway
Correct. Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is first-line chronic management of Wolff-Parkinson-White, removing the substrate for reentry and pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
Lifelong oral adenosine
Adenosine is intravenous, acts for seconds and is dangerous in pre-excited atrial fibrillation; it cannot be long-term therapy.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms and does not stop conduction down an accessory pathway.

opts: Aspirin alone
Aspirin is an antiplatelet drug, not one of the anticoagulants listed for atrial fibrillation.
None, given her age
Older age raises stroke risk rather than ruling out anticoagulation; a high score means she typically needs it.
A direct oral anticoagulant
Correct. Direct oral anticoagulants (dabigatran, apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) are preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation; a high stroke-risk score means she needs anticoagulation.
Warfarin as first choice
Warfarin is an alternative with a target ratio of 2 to 3, but direct oral anticoagulants are preferred in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.

opts: No urgent care is usually needed
Correct. If a vagal maneuver terminates nodal reentry in a patient who has been educated, urgent medical attention is usually not required.
Come to the emergency department
An emergency visit is not needed once an educated patient has terminated the episode and feels well.
Start an anticoagulant
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; nodal reentry does not require it.
Arrange a pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms such as sick sinus syndrome; nodal reentry stopped at home needs no device.

opts: Adenosine
Adenosine comes second, after a vagal maneuver fails, in stable supraventricular tachycardia.
Intravenous amiodarone
Amiodarone is tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, not as the first step in a stable narrow complex tachycardia.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is reserved for the unstable patient; she is stable, so a vagal maneuver comes first.
Vagal maneuver
Correct. Stable supraventricular tachycardia is treated first with a vagal maneuver, then adenosine (up to twice), keeping synchronized cardioversion for instability.

opts: Start an anticoagulant
Nodal reentry does not raise stroke risk the way atrial fibrillation does; no anticoagulant is needed.
Expect a pacemaker
A pacemaker is for slow rhythms; nodal reentry is a tachycardia managed with trigger avoidance and vagal maneuvers.
Limit caffeine and alcohol
Correct. Nodal reentry may occur spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists and sympathomimetics, so limiting her known triggers is sensible counseling.
Avoid all exercise
Exertion can trigger episodes, but blanket exercise avoidance is not the advice; limiting caffeine, alcohol and stimulants is.

opts: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block
Flutter with fixed 2:1 block is regular with sawtooth waves; his rhythm is irregularly irregular.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia keeps a normal P wave before every beat at 60 to 100; he has no P waves at 132.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. An irregularly irregular narrow complex rhythm with absent P waves is atrial fibrillation, and hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnea and older age are listed risk factors.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but keeps P waves, in at least three shapes; his tracing has none.

set2.q: A 67-year-old man has had three recurrences of atrial flutter, and rate control has been hard to achieve. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Catheter ablation
Correct. Ablation is the definitive management of atrial flutter, which has a substantial recurrence rate and is harder to rate-control than fibrillation.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; recurrent flutter is cured by ablating its circuit.
Septal myectomy
Myectomy relieves outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it does not treat flutter.
Carotid endarterectomy
Carotid surgery treats carotid stenosis; recurrent flutter is referred for catheter ablation.

set2.q: A 21-year-old man collapses while playing basketball and arrives with a very fast regular tachycardia. He is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70. A vagal maneuver fails, and adenosine slows the rate to reveal an irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes, each with a delta wave (slurred upstroke). Which is the next step?
opts: Oral metoprolol
An oral beta blocker is too slow and, as a nodal blocker, leaves the accessory pathway unopposed; procainamide is the drug used.
Intravenous procainamide

Correct. When slowing from adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, intravenous procainamide is used and adenosine is never repeated: nodal blockade leaves the accessory pathway unopposed.
A second dose of adenosine
More adenosine blocks only the normal node, leaving the accessory pathway free to conduct the fibrillation at rates approaching 300.
Intravenous atropine
Atropine speeds conduction and treats unstable bradycardia; it would make a pre-excited tachycardia faster.

set2.q: A 38-year-old woman has recurrent, symptomatic focal atrial tachycardia despite an oral beta blocker. She wants a definitive option. Referral for which procedure is most appropriate?
opts: Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; an ectopic atrial focus driving a tachycardia is cured by ablation.
Repeated adenosine
Adenosine usually fails to terminate focal atrial tachycardia and has no long-term role.
Lifelong anticoagulation
Anticoagulation prevents stroke in atrial fibrillation and flutter; it does not treat a focal atrial tachycardia.
Catheter ablation
Correct. Catheter ablation of the ectopic focus is usually curative for focal atrial tachycardia (about 90%), after oral beta blockers or calcium channel blockers as initial therapy.

set2.q: A 28-year-old woman has sudden palpitations after three energy drinks. She notices her neck throbbing, and examination shows a frog sign (rapid visible pulsations in the neck). Her heart rate is 172 and regular, with a narrow QRS and no visible P waves. She has no heart disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia shows a normal P wave before each QRS and rarely exceeds 160; hers has hidden P waves at 172 with sudden onset.
Atrioventricular nodal reentry

Correct. A paroxysmal, regular narrow tachycardia with hidden P waves, neck pulsations (the frog sign) and a stimulant trigger in a young woman without heart disease is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular with three or more P-wave shapes in acutely ill lung or heart patients.
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; her rhythm is regular, which points to nodal reentry.

set2.q: A 34-year-old man has occasional premature junctional contractions (early narrow beats with no visible P wave) on a monitor and is anxious about them. He has no symptoms and no heart disease. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Catheter ablation
Catheter ablation has no role in occasional, benign premature junctional beats that cause no symptoms.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms from block or sinus failure, not occasional early beats.
Reassurance; no treatment
Correct. No treatment is needed if premature junctional contractions are asymptomatic and infrequent, and reassurance of the benign nature of the rhythm is often adequate.
Metoprolol for life
A beta blocker such as metoprolol is for persistent symptoms or frequent beats; he has neither.

set2.q: A 68-year-old man is brought in confused, with a blood pressure of 76/40. The monitor shows a slow, regular rhythm at 36 with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Which is the first-line treatment?
opts: Adenosine
Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node to stop supraventricular tachycardia; in a slow, unstable rhythm it would deepen the bradycardia.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is a timed shock for an unstable tachycardia with a pulse; unstable bradycardia is treated with atropine first.
Permanent pacemaker
A permanent pacemaker is definitive care for chronic symptomatic bradycardia; the acutely unstable patient first gets atropine, then temporary pacing.
Atropine

Correct. Acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable sinus bradycardia is treated first with atropine; if it fails, a temporary pacemaker follows, and chronic symptomatic disease gets a permanent one.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with an exacerbation and respiratory failure. His pulse is 128 and irregular. The electrocardiogram shows a P wave before every QRS, with at least three different P-wave shapes in lead II. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves at all; his rhythm has a P wave before every QRS, in three shapes.
Focal atrial tachycardia
Focal atrial tachycardia is regular, with one consistent abnormal P wave from a single focus, not three shapes.
Atrial flutter, variable block
Flutter shows uniform sawtooth waves at 250 or more; his discrete P waves in three different shapes point to multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia

Correct. An irregular tachycardia with a P wave for every QRS and at least three distinct P-wave shapes in one lead is multifocal atrial tachycardia, usually from severe lung disease or heart failure in an acutely ill patient.

set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure has atrial flutter (sawtooth flutter waves) with a ventricular rate of 140. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/78 and no chest pain. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Adenosine twice
Adenosine is used for reentrant supraventricular tachycardia; stable flutter is rate-controlled.
Permanent pacemaker
A pacemaker treats slow rhythms; flutter at 140 needs rate control with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.
A beta or calcium channel blocker
Correct. Hemodynamically stable atrial flutter is rate-controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker; rate control is the first goal, though harder to achieve than in fibrillation.
Synchronized cardioversion
Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable flutter; she is stable, so rate control comes first.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with sick sinus syndrome has pauses on monitoring that alternate with runs of ventricular tachycardia. Which device is indicated?
opts: Ablation alone
Ablation does not fix the failing sinus node behind the pauses; the device answer is a pacemaker with a defibrillator.
Pacemaker-defibrillator
Correct. Tachy-brady syndrome often needs a permanent pacemaker, and when the tachyarrhythmia is ventricular tachycardia the patient needs a pacemaker with an implantable cardioverter defibrillator.
Pacemaker alone
A pacemaker alone protects against pauses but cannot shock ventricular tachycardia; a defibrillator must be added.
No device; observe
Observation suits pauses that cause no symptoms; ventricular tachycardia alternating with pauses needs a pacemaker with a defibrillator.
